questions.q: Why could the nightly-report CronJob's container allocate memory without any ceiling?
options: It had no resources.limits block at all, so nothing inside Kubernetes told the kernel to stop its memory growth earlier
CronJobs are exempt from resource limits by design
Its memory limit was accidentally set far too high, not missing
Only CPU limits matter for memory-related incidents like this one
questions.explain: With no memory limit set, the container has no ceiling and keeps allocating as long as the node has free memory.

questions.q: What is the real difference between order-worker showing OOMKilled and order-api showing Evicted in this incident?
options: There is no real difference -- both terms describe the exact same mechanism
Evicted only happens to Deployments, OOMKilled only happens to CronJobs
OOMKilled means the pod's own manifest was misconfigured; Evicted means the node ran out of disk space
OOMKilled is the kernel's OOMKiller killing a specific process; Evicted is the kubelet proactively removing a pod to relieve node-wide memory pressure before the kernel intervenes
questions.explain: They are two different mechanisms responding to the same underlying memory pressure: one kernel-level, one kubelet-level.

questions.q: Why did order-worker and order-api fail even though their own manifests had correct resource settings?
options: They were sharing a node with the unlimited report container, and a neighbor's uncapped memory use can destabilize every pod on that node, not just itself
Their own resources.limits values were actually too low, which was the real cause
They had been scheduled on a node with no memory at all
Kubernetes periodically kills random healthy pods regardless of resource settings
questions.explain: A pod's own correct configuration doesn't protect it from a neighbor on the same node with no memory ceiling at all.

questions.q: What does setting requests (not just limits) actually influence?
options: Requests have no real effect and exist only for documentation purposes
Requests only affect billing, not scheduling or behavior
What the scheduler uses to decide which node has room for a pod -- a pod with no requests can be packed too tightly for its real usage
Requests set a hard ceiling identical to limits
questions.explain: The scheduler places pods based on requests; a pod with none can be placed as if it needs almost nothing, regardless of real usage.

questions.q: What does a namespace-level LimitRange fix that correcting the one CronJob manifest alone doesn't?
options: It automatically rewrites every existing Deployment's YAML files in the repository
It prevents any future engineer's container that omits a resources block from running completely unbounded, by supplying default requests/limits automatically on admission
It removes the need for resources blocks in any manifest ever again
It only applies retroactively to pods that already failed
questions.explain: A LimitRange supplies safe default requests/limits to any container that doesn't declare its own, catching the next engineer's mistake automatically.
